claim: After occupying Gaza in 1967, Israel tolerated and at times funded the Islamist movement there as a counterweight to the secular Palestine Liberation Organization and Fatah. The Israeli military governor of Gaza, Brigadier General Yitzhak Segev, told New York Times correspondent David K. Shipler in 1981 that he financed religious activists out of his budget; Shipler later wrote that Segev described financing the Islamic movement as a counter to the PLO and the communists. Sheikh Ahmed Yassin's charity Mujama al-Islamiya, licensed by Israel in 1979, was the organizational seedbed from which Hamas formed in 1987 at the start of the First Intifada. Avner Cohen, the Israeli official who had handled religious affairs in Gaza, told the Wall Street Journal in 2009: "Hamas, to my great regret, is Israel's creation." The stronger claim that "Israel created Hamas" is contested and overstated: Hamas grew out of the Muslim Brotherhood and became an armed movement on its own; Israel funded the precursor charity, not the militant organization, and Palestinian and Israeli sources note the "creation" framing has been used by both sides for opposing political ends. What is documented is the early Israeli policy of building up the Islamists against the secular nationalists.

sources.label: David K. Shipler, The New York Times (1981) — Yitzhak Segev, then Israel's military governor of Gaza, on funding religious activists. The closest primary statement to the "Israel financed the Islamists" claim.
